claim: Standard-quantum-limit (shot-noise) optical energy per MAC for homodyne photoelectric-multiplication ONNs, MNIST MLPs, from simulation
value: 0.5-1 aJ (5-10 photons) at N=100; 50-100 zJ (0.5-1 photon) at N=1000
locator: arXiv v2, Sec. 'Deep Learning at the Standard Quantum Limit', Fig. 2(c) discussion
quote: This is around 0.5–1 aJ (5–10 photons) for the small network (inner layer size N = 100), and 50–100 zJ (0.5–1 photon) for the large network (inner layer size N = 1000).
notes: Hamerly et al., PRX 9, 021032 (2019). Simulated (not measured); network-dependent; perfect detectors; counts input optical energy only. Per-MAC photons fall as 1/N because the per-detector count N*n_mac stays >>1 (paper: 'the number of photons per detector N nmac is typically >> 1'). Realistic devices shift this up by (eta_d eta_c eta_s beta_mod)^-1, which the authors put at <~10.

claim: The SQL is set by quadrature-measurement uncertainty on coherent states: temperature- and device-independent, an absolute lower bound for this ONN class
locator: arXiv v2, Sec. 'Deep Learning at the Standard Quantum Limit'
quote: the intrinsic uncertainty of quadrature measurements on coherent states [43], which is temperature- and device-independent. This should be viewed as an absolute lower bound for the energy consumption of neural networks of this type
notes: Squeezed light could beat it but the authors expect a net energy increase (squeezing all inputs incl. vacuum ports). This is the physics basis of D11 in docs/DERIVATIONS.md.

claim: Landauer (thermodynamic) limit per irreversible bit operation at room temperature
locator: arXiv v2, Sec. 'Deep Learning at the Standard Quantum Limit', energy-budget paragraph (Fig. 3c)
quote: in non-reversible logic gates is bounded by the Landauer (thermodynamic) limit Eop = kT log(2) ≈ 3 zJ [71].

claim: Landauer limit for a digital 32-bit MAC (~10^3 irreversible gates), vs the optical SQL
quote: and each bit operation consumes at least kT log(2), giving a limit Emac ≥ 3 aJ (dotted line in Fig. 3(c)). This is already higher than the SQL for the larger networks with N ≥ 100.
notes: Gate count per 32-bit multiply ~1e3 (paper text; exponent lost in PDF extraction, so not quoted).

claim: Landauer limit for an 8-bit digital multiply (most efficient multiplier, Wallace/Booth)
locator: Supplementary Sec. S5 'Landauer Limit Dependence on Architecture and Bit Precision'
quote: By moving from 32-bit arithmetic to 8-bit arithmetic, the Landauer limit decreases by a factor of 16. For the most efficient multiplier under this metric (Wallace/Booth), it reaches just under 100 zJ/MAC (10−19 J/MAC).
notes: The 8-bit digital Landauer floor (~0.1 aJ) is ~10^5 below the 8-bit optical shot-noise floor per READ (8.4-9.9 fJ, R8-127) and ~24x below the per-MAC optical floor at N*T=4096 (DERIVED: 9.94 fJ/4096 = 2.43 aJ; 2.43/0.1 = 24). Neither floor is binding in practice.

claim: Why optics can beat Landauer: analog operation and reversible interference
quote: (1) it operates in analog, avoiding the overhead of many bit operations per multiplication, and (2) the matrix product is performed through optical interference, which is reversible and not subject to the bound.
notes: Detection (photon->charge) is still irreversible and is where the SQL enters.

claim: Detector capacitance needed for shot-noise-limited (not Johnson-limited) read-out, C0 = N*n_mac*e^2/(2kT)
locator: Supplementary Sec. S4, Eq. (S18) and Table S1
quote: From these figures, we see that C0 is in the few-femtofarad range, sub-femtofarad receiverless detectors should be able to reach the SQL, while larger detectors will be limited by Johnson noise.
notes: Table S1: small NN 1.6-24 fF, large NN 1.2-3.2 fF. Measured detector capacitances: 0.08 fF estimated (R8-054), <1 fF (R8-057), 2 fF integrated node (R8-059), ~10 fF commercial Ge incl. parasitics (R8-055).

claim: Cooling the chip to cut Johnson noise gives no net energy gain once the Carnot cost of removing the heat is counted
quote: Since this lower limit to dQh is independent of Tc , reducing Johnson noise by lowering the chip temperature does not confer any benefit in total energy efficiency.
notes: Relevant to branch E: a cold orbital environment does not lower the photonic energy floor unless heat is rejected at the cold temperature for free; radiator area grows as T^-4 (D10).

claim: Near-term per-neuron electronics estimate for homodyne ONN (TIA ~100 fJ, ADC few pJ/sample)
locator: arXiv v2, Fig. 3(c) paragraph on detector electronics
quote: Thus a reasonable near-term estimate would be few-pJ/neuron; this figure is divided by the number of inputs per neuron to give the energy per MAC
notes: Paper cites TIAs at ~100 fJ and ADCs at few-pJ/sample. Compare measured 2023-26: TIA 165 fJ/read (R8-052), ADC 1.06-4.19 pJ/conversion (R8-060..R8-063).

claim: Weight encoding cost in photoelectric-multiplication ONNs: one weight pulse per MAC, divided by the batch fan-out B
value: >=1 fJ (modulator) to >1 pJ (with driver + memory), divided by B
locator: arXiv v2, last paragraph of Fig. 3(c) discussion
quote: There is one weight pulse per MAC, so at the minimum this will be 1 fJ/MAC for the modulator, and may rise above 1 pJ/MAC once the driver electronics and memory access are included.
notes: Same paragraph: 'it can be fanned out to many neural networks in parallel, reducing this cost by a factor of B, the batch size.' This weight-encoding term is ABSENT from D13 (see R8-129).

claim: Measured ONN accuracy vs detected photons per multiplication (free-space OLED/SLM, 4-layer MLP, MNIST)
quote: achieving 99% accuracy on handwritten-digit classification using ∼3.2 detected photons per weight multiplication and ∼90% accuracy using ∼0.64 photons (∼2.4 × 10−19 J of optical energy) per weight multiplication.
notes: Wang et al., Nat. Commun. 2022. Detected optical energy only: sub-photon levels were reached by attenuation (neutral-density filters), not by an efficient source; SLM transmission ~46%. Evaluated on the first 130 MNIST test images.

claim: Measured dot-product error at 0.001 photons per multiplication on ~0.5-million-element vectors
value: ~6% RMS (= 4 noise-equivalent bits); ~0.2% (~9 bits) at >=2 photons/MAC
quote: With 0.001 photons per scalar multiplication, the error was measured to be ∼6% (Figure 2b; see Supplementary Information Section 12 for the details of RMS-error calculation); the dominant contribution to this error was from shot noise at the detector
notes: Same section: 'an analog RMS error of 6% corresponds to 4 bits, and 0.2% RMS error corresponds to ∼9 bits'. Integration time ~100 ns (>=10 MHz), not GHz.

claim: Photons per READ in the sub-photon experiment: 0.001 photons/MAC x 505,521 MACs per dot product
quote: we measured the numerical precision of dot products between vectors each of size ∼0.5 million.
notes: DERIVED: 0.001 x 505,521 = 506 photons; 1/sqrt(506) = 4.4% vs 6% measured. Sub-photon PER MAC is a fan-in effect: the precision budget is per READ (D11: 4^b photons per read), not per MAC. 4 bits needs 256 photons per read.

claim: Detected optical energy per MNIST inference at 99% accuracy (89,400 MACs)
quote: To achieve an accuracy of 99%, the total optical energy detected for each inference of a handwritten digit was ∼1 pJ (Figure 3b).
notes: Optical energy only; no laser wall-plug, modulator, detector electronics or memory.

claim: Netcast (delocalised photonic DNN): measured optical energy per multiply at 98.8% MNIST; <1 photon/multiply with single-photon detectors
quote: We demonstrate operation in a photon-starved environment with 40 aJ/multiply of optical energy for 98.8% accurate image recognition and <1 photon/multiply using single photon detectors.
notes: Sludds et al. (Science 2022). Optical energy at the receiver only.

claim: Measured sensitivity of custom time-integrating receivers (integrate M=100 timesteps before read-out)
quote: Our custom time-integrating receivers, shown on the left of Fig. 4(a), boost the measured signal by M at readout, increasing the voltage SNR by M and enabling receivers operating with ≈10 aJ/MAC (≈100 photons) of optical energy.
notes: Time integration demonstrated at M = 100 (>= the T = 32 used in E015). Same paragraph: amplified photoreceivers ~10-100 fJ/MAC (dash lost in PDF text), amplified linear APDs ~1 fJ/MAC.

claim: Sensitivity of amplified linear-mode APD receivers in the same comparison
quote: Amplified linear mode avalanche photodetectors, shown in the middle of Fig. 4(a), overcome some of the thermal noise of the amplifier and achieve ≈1fJ/MAC.
notes: Thermal-noise-limited amplified receivers sit 2-4 orders above the ~10 aJ/MAC integrating receiver.

claim: Clock rate of the <1-photon/MAC SNSPD experiment
quote: For our experimental demonstrations using the single photon detectors we clock the system at 30kHz, allowing us to operate away from the dark counts of the detectors
notes: Negative caveat: the sub-photon regime was shown at kHz, limited by SNSPD saturation (~100 fW) and dark counts, and at cryogenic temperature.

claim: Netcast projected client energy with N = M = 100 fan-out and time integration
quote: Assuming near-term values of N = M = 100, client energy consumption can reach ≈10 fJ/MAC
notes: Scaling (1/N) pJ/MAC for input encoding + (1/M) pJ/MAC for integrator/ADC. Excludes the server's weight transmission.

claim: Stochastic single-photon-detection ONN: MNIST accuracy vs photons per MAC (hidden layer at SNR~1)
quote: with a test accuracy of 98% using an optical neural network with a hidden layer operating in the single-photon regime; the optical energy used to perform the classification corresponds to just 0.038 photons per multiply–accumulate (MAC) operation.
notes: Ma et al. Requires physics-aware stochastic training; only one hidden layer is single-photon; optical energy only.

claim: Fan-in, not optics per se, fixes the optical energy per dot product; optoelectronic (electrical) fan-in can match it
quote: the amount of optical energy needed to achieve a particular signal-to-noise ratio for a vector-vector dot product is fixed regardless of the vector size—but similar efficiency can be achieved with optoelectronic fan-in
notes: McMahon, 'The physics of optical computing' (Nat. Rev. Phys. 2023). Negative for photonics-only claims: sub-photon/MAC is an analog-summation advantage.

claim: O/E and A/D conversion costs can make an optical processor less efficient than an all-electronic one
locator: arXiv v1, Sec. on design strategies, item 1
quote: these costs may be so large that they don’t just dominate the total energy cost of the optical processor, but make the energy cost so high that the processor is less energy efficient than an all-electronic processor.
notes: Consistent with the only measured full-stack photonic AI processor (R3-043/R3-045: 318x system/core).

claim: Receiverless detection: a ~300 aF total node turns 260 aC of photo-charge into a ~0.8 V logic swing, removing the receiver amplifier
locator: arXiv v3, Sec. 'Low-capacitance front ends and receiverless operation'
quote: That would completely eliminate the 170 fJ/bit of receiver circuit energy, allowing the receiving system to operate at ~ 1 fJ/bit total energy.
notes: Miller, 'Attojoule Optoelectronics...' (JLT 2017). 300 aF includes PD + wiring + transistor gate: no demonstrated node that small (best measured integrated node 2 fF, R8-059).

claim: Conventional low-energy photoreceiver cited by Miller: energy and sensitivity with ~30 fF input capacitance
value: 170 fJ/bit at 25 Gb/s; -14.9 dBm (~1.3 fJ/bit optical)
quote: This example gives a receiver circuit operating at 170 fJ/bit at 25 Gb/s with -14.9 dBm noise-limited sensitivity.
notes: Second-hand (Miller reporting ref. [112]). Electrical receiver energy is ~130x the optical energy it detects.

claim: Shot-noise photon statistics for binary links: 20-100 photons per bit; 100 aJ/bit at ~1 eV = ~600 photons
quote: For ~ 1 eV photons, a received optical energy of 100 aJ/bit corresponds to ~ 600 photons/bit, so at such a level we are likely far from shot noise being a significant problem.
notes: Binary detection needs far fewer photons than multi-level analog: 4-bit analog read needs 4^4 = 256, 8-bit 65,536 (D11).

claim: kT/C thermal noise on a detector node, independent of the charging resistor: sqrt(kT/C)
quote: the resulting fluctuation of the voltage on the capacitor is essentially independent of the resistor value
notes: DERIVED at 300 K: v_n = sqrt(kB*T/C); q_n = sqrt(kB*T*C)/e. Compare with the shot noise of the 4^b photo-electrons: 8-bit sqrt(65,536) = 256 e- dominates kTC for every C <= 10 fF; 4-bit sqrt(256) = 16 e- is EXCEEDED by kTC for C >~ 1.6 fF, so a 4-bit read on a 2 fF node needs 443 e- not 256 (R8-128; script evidence/sources/R8/_derive_r8.py).

claim: Analog power grows exponentially with bit resolution; efficiency 'futile' ~6 bits, 'non-viable' ~10 bits
quote: On the other hand, the power needed to generate an analog signal scales exponentially with its bit resolution [34]. In other words, the endeavor for energy efficiency rapidly becomes futile around 6 bits and then strictly non-viable around 10 bits.
notes: Tait (NIST). Opinion-level threshold, but consistent with 4^b (shot) / 2^b (thermal) photon scaling.

claim: Laser pump power per resolution bit in an analog photonic link: thermal-noise regime (SFDR convention)
locator: arXiv v1, Sec. III.B, thermal regime (Eq. 17)
quote: Strikingly, the power-resolution scaling rate of 15 log 2 = 4.5 dB/bit is less than that of any analog electrical link: 20 log 2 = 6.0 dB/bit.
notes: Bits here are SFDR-based (third-order intermodulation), stricter than the SNR bits of D11. SNR convention: thermal-limited optical power grows 2^b (3 dB/bit), shot-limited 4^b (6 dB/bit).

claim: Laser pump power per resolution bit: shot-noise regime (SFDR convention)
locator: arXiv v1, Sec. III.B, shot regime (Eq. 20-21)
quote: The result is a strong resolution scaling of 30 log 2 = 9.0 dB/bit instead of 20 log 2 = 6.0 dB/bit in analog electronics.
notes: APD gain strictly increases shot-limited power (excess noise F_A > 1), per the same paragraph.

claim: Per-channel pump-energy metric, thermal-noise limit (R_PD 0.8 A/W, C_pd 35 fF, 300 K, 1550 nm)
locator: Table II 'Laser pump power metrics for single-channel analog photonic links', row Thermal E_thrm
quote: Thermal Ethrm 820×10−3 6.5 52 420 fJ
notes: SFDR-convention bits; 35 fF baseline detector. Not directly comparable to D11 (SNR convention).

claim: Per-channel pump-energy metric, shot-noise physical limit
locator: Table II, row Shot E_shot (physical limit)
quote: Shot Eshot (physical limit) 15×10−3 0.96 61 3.9×103 fJ
notes: SFDR convention: 8-bit shot limit 3.9 pJ is ~460x the SNR-convention floor of D11 at the same 1550 nm (65,536 photons = 8.40 fJ). The choice of 'bits' convention moves the floor by >2 orders of magnitude; D11 (SNR) is the optimistic one.

claim: Laser relative-intensity-noise (RIN) limit on analog resolution vs bandwidth (RIN -155 dB/Hz, SFDR convention)
value: 7.5 bits @1 GHz; 5.3 bits @100 GHz; 8 bits only up to 410 MHz
locator: arXiv v1, Sec. III.B, RIN regime (Eq. 22-25)
quote: Stated as a bandwidth limit: at 4 bits, the maximum frequency is 1.7 THz; at 6 bits, it is 26 GHz; at 8 bits, it is 410 MHz.
notes: Preceding sentence: 'The resolution limit is 7.5 effective bits at 1 GHz and 5.3 bits at 100 GHz.' Independent of laser power. Could be relaxed by balanced detection, which the author calls challenging.

claim: RIN limit in the SNR convention: SNR = 1/(RIN*B), ENOB = (SNR_dB - 1.76)/6.02, RIN = -155 dB/Hz
value: 8.8 bits @10 GHz; 11.3 bits @312.5 MHz (10 GHz / T=32); 7.6 bits @56 GHz
quote: RIN imposes a hard limit on the ability of laser light to represent analog signals.
notes: DERIVED: SNR_dB = 155 - 10 log10(B). 10 GHz: 55.0 dB -> 8.84 bits; 0.3125 GHz: 70.1 -> 11.34; 56 GHz: 47.5 -> 7.60. Time integration over T narrows the read bandwidth and relaxes RIN. Tait's SFDR convention (R8-032) is ~4 bits stricter. Which convention applies to NN accuracy is an OPEN question.

claim: Readout ADC power per added output bit in the thermal-noise-limited regime (Lightmatter photonic processor authors)
locator: Supplementary Information, Sec. VI 'Comparative Analysis of Photonic Processors'
quote: This equation is valid in the thermal noise-limited regime (where our ADC and many high-performance ADCs operate).
notes: Exponent '2^(2 dB)' reconstructed from the raw PDF text (superscript lost in extraction: 'scales as , 2 2 ∆𝐵'). x4 per bit matches the 4^b photon floor scaling.

claim: Calibration cadence of the only measured full-stack photonic AI processor (Lightmatter, 4x128x128 PTC)
locator: Supplementary Information, Sec. V 'Photonic Tensor Core Calibration'
quote: Calibration is performed once per hour, a frequency determined heuristically to balance performance stability and computational overhead.
notes: 10 calibration steps (LPR, VSTAB, WMOD, VMOD, TIA+VADC) run on an on-chip RISC-V control processor. Calibration energy/time not reported.

claim: Silicon microring modulator (self-biased, zero DC bias): energy per bit at 32 Gb/s NRZ, 0.43 Vpp, error-free over 2 km
quote: the device supports error-free 32-Gbps NRZ transmission over 2-km SSMF with only 0.43-Vpp drive and zero electrical bias, yielding energy efficiency of 0.97 fJ/bit without DSP.
notes: Drive and BER measured; energy calculated as ~C*V^2/4 with ESTIMATED Cj = 21 fF (R8-037); modulator only, no driver/DAC, no heater lock (R8-038). DERIVED check: 21e-15*0.43^2/4 = 0.97 fJ. Same device: 0.78 fJ/bit PAM4 at 0.73 Vpp; 16 fJ/bit NRZ at 2 Vpp under -3 V bias.

claim: Si microring modulator junction capacitance used for the fJ/bit figure
quote: The junction capacitance Cj of out MRM is estimated to be 21 fF under zero electrical-bias and decreased to 16 fF under a -3 V electrical-bias.
notes: 'out' is a typo in the source (= our). Estimated, not measured.

claim: Si microring thermal tuning efficiency (resonance lock needs heater power, excluded from the fJ/bit)
quote: shown in Fig. 3c, where the red-shift is ~81.2 pm/mW.
notes: Wafer-level spread 77.6-84.5 pm/mW (Supplementary). Holding a ring on resonance costs mW-scale static power per ring unless athermal.

claim: Si microring modulator built on a 300-mm silicon photonics line with wafer-scale uniformity
quote: trench-integrated structure on a 300-mm silicon photonic platform, achieving both outstanding device performance and remarkable wafer-scale uniformity.
notes: Zhangjiang Laboratory, Shanghai. Also: open eyes to 400 Gb/s PAM6 in depletion mode.

claim: Thin-film lithium niobate MZM (low-k underfill): electrical energy per bit at 390 Gb/s PAM8
locator: arXiv, Sec. on data transmission (energy paragraph)
quote: an electrical Vrms of 245.6 mV (97.6 mV) is used for the 390 Gbit/s data modulation in the C-band (O-band), corresponding to an electrical energy consumption of 4.42 fJ/bit (0.69 fJ/bit)
notes: Computed by the authors as Vrms^2/(B*R) with measured Vrms and driver impedance R (50 ohm): power dissipated in the termination, excl. the driver/DAC that makes the swing. Includes probe and cable loss.

claim: TFLN MZM half-wave voltage and bandwidth (7 mm long)
value: Vpi 1.9 V (C) / 1.54 V (O); 1.33 / 1.08 V*cm; 220 GHz extrapolated 3-dB BW
quote: The fabricated 7-mm-long modulator exhibits a low half-wave voltage Vπ of 1.9 V at C-band and 1.54 V at O-band
notes: Bandwidth is extrapolated (not measured) beyond instrument range.

claim: TFLN energy per analog SYMBOL (PAM8 = 3 bits/symbol at 130 GBd)
quote: High-speed data transmission in both C- and O-bands using the same device has been demonstrated for the first time by PAM8 with data rates up to 390 Gbit/s
notes: DERIVED: 0.69 fJ/bit x 3 = 2.07; 4.42 x 3 = 13.26 fJ/symbol. Photonic MVM pays per symbol (one analog level per input), not per bit.

claim: Plasmonic-organic MZM at 4 K: electrical energy per bit at 16 Gb/s with 96 mV drive
quote: Having an estimated device capacitance of 25 fF of the plasmonic MZM including RF pads, the electrical energy consumption for 16 GBd 2PAM with a V PP,50Ω of 96 mV is as low as 230 aJ/bit
notes: ACS Photonics 2024 (OA). Cryogenic (4 K); BER only below SD-FEC at 96 mV; capacitance estimated.

claim: Plasmonic MZM at 4 K at higher rates
quote: for 128 GBd 2PAM with a V PP,50Ω of 1.0 V, the E bit is 25 fJ/bit, and for 80 GBd 4PAM with a V PP,50Ω of 897 mV, the E bit is 5.6 fJ/bit.
notes: Same estimated 25 fF. Plasmonic ring modulator (O-band): 13 fJ/bit at 128/180 GBd (assumed 13 fF).

claim: Plasmonic propagation loss (80 nm MIM slot), room temperature vs 4 K
locator: Results, 'Plasmonic Propagation Losses at Cryogenic Temperatures'
quote: It is found that the plasmonic propagation losses decrease from 0.52 dB/μm at 296 K (room temperature) to 0.27 dB/μm at 4 K.
notes: On-chip device loss of the plasmonic MZM estimated at 5.9 dB (same paper). A 5.9 dB modulator adds ~4x to the laser term; attojoule drive energy is bought with optical loss.

claim: Injection-locked VCSEL modulator (coherent VCSEL ONN): electro-optic energy per symbol
value: <5 aJ/symbol; Vpi 4 mV; up to 25 GS/s
quote: exhibit high EO conversion (<5 attojoule/symbol with Vπ =4 mV), high operation bandwidth (up to 25 GS/s), and compact footprint (<0.01 mm2 per device).
notes: Chen et al. (Nat. Photon. 2023). Modulation power Vpi^2/R_VCSEL = 3.7 nW (R_VCSEL 4.3 kohm): the laser bias itself (390 uW) dominates, see R8-048.

claim: VCSEL ONN 'full-system' energy per operation
quote: The full-system energy efficiency and compute density reach 7 femtojoules per operation (fJ/OP) and 25 TeraOP/(mm2 · s)
notes: Not a wall-plug measurement: Supplementary Table I sums measured optics (2.5 fJ/OP) with literature ADC ~1 pJ/use, TIA ~1 pJ/use, DAC ~0.5 pJ/use, memory ~100 fJ/access, amortised over 9x9 fan-out and 28x28 time integration.

claim: VCSEL ONN measured optical energy per operation, incl. electrical power for laser generation and data modulation
quote: Our optical energy efficiency of 2.5 fJ/OP is 140× and 1000× better than the state-of-the-art integrated ONN
notes: Includes VCSEL bias power (wall-plug) and fan-out j = 9x9; excludes electronics.

claim: Wall-plug efficiency of the VCSELs used in the VCSEL ONN
quote: The wall plug efficiency is ξ = Pi /Pb = 25 %.
notes: P_b = V_b x I_b = 390 uW per VCSEL.

claim: Monolithic optical receiver front end (TIA + post-amp): measured power, noise and energy per bit at 112 Gb/s (56 GBd PAM4)
value: 9.22 mW; 737 nA rms IRNC; 29.5 GHz; 0.08 pJ/bit
quote: consuming 9.22 mW of power from a 1.2 V supply. The measured circuit achieves 61.5 dBW transimpedance gain and 29.5 GHz electrical BW with less than 737 nA RMS integrated input referred noise current and 0.08 pJ/bit.
notes: Georgia Tech. Electrical eyes measured; photodiode modelled. 2.5 mW at 0.9 V supports 32 GBd.

claim: Receiver sensitivity computed from the measured input-referred noise (OOK, BER 1e-12, no FEC)
quote: We compute a minimum sensitivty of -21.3 dBm with standard forward error correction (KP-FEC) technqiues and -19.57 dBm without FEC.
notes: Typos are the source's. Computed (Q*i_rms/R), not a BER measurement. -19.57 dBm = 11 uW; at 56 GBd that is ~0.2 fJ optical per symbol (DERIVED).

claim: TIA electrical energy per analog read (per symbol)
quote: we determine the maximum bit rate to be 112 Gbps with the 56 GBaud PAM-4 signaling, corresponding to 0.08 pJ/bit.
notes: DERIVED: 9.22 mW / 56e9 symbols/s = 164.6 fJ per symbol. TIA-limited optical energy per read (737 nA rms, 0.93 A/W, 29.5 GHz, sigma <= FS/2^b incl. shot): 0.25 fJ (4-bit, 1,654 photons at 1310 nm) and 12.9 fJ (8-bit, 85,148 photons): the 8-bit case is shot-noise dominated.

claim: Monolithic receiver front end fabricated on GlobalFoundries Fotonix
quote: The circuit, fabricated on the GlobalFoundries FotonixTM monolithic silicon photonics platform, is characterized by its DC operation, AC operation, noise characteristics, and time domain behavior.
notes: Monolithic PD+TIA integration is available on a commercial line (MPW access via GF).

claim: Ge-on-Si asymmetric Fabry-Perot nano-photodetector: capacitance, dark current, responsivity, speed at 1315.5 nm
quote: We demonstrated a Germanium-on-Silicon photodetector utilizing an asymmetric-Fabry-Perot resonator with 0.08 fF capacitance. The measurements at 1315.5 nm show 0.72 nA (3.40 nA) dark current, 0.93 A/W (0.96 A/W) responsivity, 36 Gb/s (38 Gb/s) operation at -1V (-2V) bias.
notes: Capacitance is ESTIMATED ('With an estimated capacitance being extremely low at 0.08 fF'); responsivity/dark current/eyes measured. Title states 91% QE (used as QE in the R8 derivation). Eyes shown without amplifier.

claim: Typical commercial silicon-photonics Ge photodetector (for comparison)
quote: today’s commercial SiPh Ge detectors have typically 15 µm2 footprint with 10 fF capacitance including parasitics and 15 nA dark current.
notes: Authors' characterisation of the commercial baseline. At 1 V a 10 fF node holds 62,400 e- ~ the 8-bit shot floor (65,536).

claim: Nano-photodetector fabricated on GlobalFoundries 45nm CMOS-SiPh (45SPCLO)
quote: AFP photodetector is fabricated on GlobalFoundries’ 45nm CMOS-SiPh platform (45SPCLO) [6]
notes: Monolithic CMOS + photonics process: detector next to transistor gate, the precondition for receiverless nodes.

claim: Photonic-crystal InGaAs nano-photodetector for amplifier-free light-to-voltage conversion (NTT)
quote: an ultracompact InGaAs PD based on a photonic crystal waveguide with a length of only 1.7 μm and a capacitance of less than 1 fF. Despite the small size of the device, a high responsivity of 1 A/W
notes: Full text not retrieved (R8-139 ACCESS-FAILED); abstract only. Resistor-loaded PD measured kV/W at GHz bandwidth without amplifier.

claim: Projected photoreceiver energy for the amplifier-free photonic-crystal PD
quote: Combined experimental and theoretical results reveal that a bandwidth in excess of 10 GHz can be expected, leading to an ultralow energy consumption of less than 1 fJ/bit for the photoreceiver.
notes: Binary (1-bit) signalling, not multi-level analog.

claim: Femtofarad O-E/E-O integration: integrated node capacitance demonstrated (NTT, photonic crystal)
quote: Here we use a photonic-crystal platform to demonstrate the first experimental proof of optoelectronic integration at only 2 fF.
notes: Abstract only (paywalled). Same work: attojoule E-O modulator, amplifier-free photoreceiver, O-E-O 'transistors' at fJ/bit. Used as C = 2 fF in the R8 derivation (best measured integrated node).

claim: Best measured ADC energy per conversion, >=4 ENOB (SNDR_hf >= 25.8 dB), 1-10 GS/s, ISSCC/VLSI 2023-2026
locator: Murmann ADC survey rev. 2026-08-01, sheet VLSI, 2026 ID C17.3
quote: An 8bit 4.8GS/s 10.9fJ/conv.-step TI-SAR ADC with 4bit/3cycle Ping-Pong Architecture and Data-Driven Zero-Overhead Background Calibration
notes: Filter (my script murmann_R8_filter.txt): year>=2023, 1e9<=fsnyq<=50e9, ENOB_hf=(SNDR_hf-1.76)/6.02. No cheaper design exists at 4-5 ENOB in the survey window: a 4-bit read pays the same ~1 pJ. Quote = survey row title.

claim: Best measured ADC energy per conversion, >=4 ENOB, 10-50 GS/s, 2023-2026
locator: Murmann survey rev. 2026-08-01, sheet VLSI, 2025 ID C8-4
quote: A PVT-Robust 16GS/s 4×TI Time-Domain ADC with Vernier-based Multipath Flash TDC achieving 25.7fJ/c-s FoM in 28nm CMOS
notes: Median of 16 designs in this bin: 6.32 pJ (DERIVED).
